ko-pha-ngan.intro: Ko Pha Ngan's great tree is a Yang Na in the village of Ban Nok, in the south of the island, a few kilometres from the Thong Sala pier. Thailand's Ministry of Culture listed it as a heritage tree of the land in 2018 and recorded a girth of 14.64 metres, a height of 53.5 metres and an age of about 400 years. It stands beside the public road, free to see, with small spirit houses at its foot.
ko-pha-ngan.meta_description: Ko Pha Ngan's giant Yang Na in Ban Nok: about 400 years old and 53.5 metres tall by Thailand's heritage tree register, free beside the road.
ko-pha-ngan.question_meta: The oldest tree on Ko Pha Ngan is the giant Yang Na of Ban Nok, about 400 years old by Thailand's heritage tree register.
ko-pha-ngan.question_answer: The oldest tree we know of on Ko Pha Ngan is the giant Yang Na in Ban Nok, in the south of the island. Thailand's Ministry of Culture put it at about 400 years when it listed the tree as a heritage tree of the land in 2018. The age is an estimate, not a count of rings.
ko-pha-ngan.question_context: The tree is a Yang Na, Dipterocarpus alatus, a tall tropical tree of the dipterocarp family. The Ministry of Culture's 2018 list of heritage trees of the land records a girth of 14.64 metres and a height of 53.5 metres, and says the tree won first prize in a 1999 Kasetsart University contest for the largest Yang Na. The register calls it the biggest Yang Na in Thailand; we have not found an independent national survey to confirm that. Other Yang Na grow around the village, and the register notes that bees nest in this one's crown. The tree stands beside the public road in Ban Nok, about 300 metres past Wat Pho in the Ban Tai area, roughly four to five kilometres from Thong Sala pier, where the ferries from Ko Samui and Surat Thani come in. It is free to see at any hour. Villagers treat it as sacred, so the spirit houses and cloth at its foot are offerings, and the low fence keeps the ground around it clear.

faq.q: Is the giant tree on Ko Pha Ngan free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. It stands beside the public road in Ban Nok, about 300 metres past Wat Pho, with no gate or fee. The road is narrow, so daylight is the better time.

faq.q: How big is the Yang Na of Ban Nok?
faq.a: Thailand's heritage tree register records a girth of 14.64 metres and a height of 53.5 metres. The girth may include the swelling at the base.

faq.q: How do I get there from Thong Sala?
faq.a: It is about four to five kilometres from Thong Sala pier, by songthaew towards Ban Tai, taxi or hired motorbike. We have not checked times or fares.

kantang.intro: Kantang, a town south-west of Trang, keeps the spot where Thailand's first rubber tree was planted, by the Ministry of Culture's account in 1901. A roadside memorial with plaques stands beside a living rubber tree on Trangkhaphum Road at the entrance to the town. Visitors report the trunk has been cut back and regrown more than once, so this is the place where Thai rubber began rather than a tree from that year.
kantang.meta_description: Thailand's first rubber tree in Kantang, Trang: a roadside memorial and living tree where rubber planting began around 1900, free to visit.
kantang.question_meta: Kantang's best-known tree is Thailand's first rubber tree, planted around 1900 by the official account, on Trangkhaphum Road.
kantang.question_answer: The tree Kantang is known for is Thailand's first rubber tree, on Trangkhaphum Road at the entrance to the town. Thailand's Ministry of Culture says the first seedling was planted here in 1901; a tourist guide says 1899. The trunk standing now may have regrown from the original, so its own age is unknown.
kantang.question_context: The Ministry of Culture listed the tree as a heritage tree of the land in 2017. Its account says the governor of Trang, Phraya Ratsadanupradit, wanted rubber seedlings from Malaya and was refused, so an official, Phra Sathonsathanphitak, brought them from Indonesia and planted the first at his residence in Kantang in 1901. The governor then trained officials and spread planting through the province, which is why he is remembered as the father of Thai rubber. A tourist guide tells it differently, with seedlings from Malaya planted in 1899 by the governor himself. Both accounts put the first tree on this spot. The register measured a tree about 20 metres tall and two metres round, in the care of Kantang municipality. Visitors have reported that the trunk has been cut back and regrown more than once, so we give it no age. The memorial is a free roadside stop with plaques, open at any hour, at the entrance to Kantang, south-west of the city of Trang.

faq.q: Is Thailand's first rubber tree still alive?
faq.a: A living rubber tree stands at the memorial, and the Ministry of Culture listed it in 2017. Visitors report the trunk has been cut back and regrown more than once, so it may have grown again from the original rather than being the 1901 trunk itself.

faq.q: When was the first rubber tree planted in Thailand?
faq.a: The Ministry of Culture says 1901, from seedlings brought from Indonesia; a tourist guide says 1899, from Malaya. Both place it here in Kantang.

faq.q: Does it cost anything to visit?
faq.a: No. It is a roadside memorial with plaques on Trangkhaphum Road, open at any hour.
